newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul finance chief seen trying to boost savings.
newsitem.headline: Seoul finance chief seen trying to boost savings.

text.p: South Korean finance minister Han Seung-soo is likely to unveil measures to encourage savings and stabilise prices when he unveils new economic policies on Tuesday, market analysts said.
The policy initiative is a response to South Korea's ballooning trade deficit, largely the result of falling international prices for the country's main exports and brisk domestic consumption.
"He will focus on inflation and he will probably talk about how to increase the savings rate in Korea," said Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Rhee said the finance minister believes "the reason Korea has a chronic current account deficit is that savings fall short of investment".
Like other analysts, however, he cautioned against expectations of major moves. "He is a very reasonable man. I don't think he'll come out with anything drastic," he said.

The announcement will be released at noon (0300 GMT) and Han will address a news conference at 2.30 p.m. (0530 GMT). The August trade deficit hit a monthly record high of $2.9 billion against a year-earlier shortfall of $901 million.
Lim Dong-seung, the president of Samsung Economic Research Insitute said the deficit was structural, and any initiatives Han announced would have little effect.

"The only ways to deal with the structural problem, in my opinion, is to freeze wages and devalue the won," Lim said. But he added he did not expect Han would address those issues. "The government has no measures to correct the overvalued won."
Falling international prices of semiconductors, steel and petroleum products lie behind Seoul's trade woes.
"The current problem is a cyclical one which Korea has no control over; it'll take time to heal," said Rhee.
Andrew Holland, head of research at BZW Securities, said: "I'm not expecting very much from the new policies because there is very little that Han can do.
"He will probably encourage people to spend less, cut down on domestic consumption, and increase savings," he said.

"The only real surprise would be if he announced Korea wasn't going to join the OECD, and I don't think that would happen." Seoul is pushing to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development this year, although there is growing domestic opposition to any moves to further open markets and exacerbate the trade deficit.

Shim Sang-dal, a fellow at the Korean Development Institute, said in the fight against inflation Han may decide to postpone utility price rises and bring down import prices by ironing out inefficiencies in the distribution system.

Imported goods are priced artificially high because large distributors and retailers have a stranglehold over key items. Shim said one way to tackle the problem would be to widen the distribution base.
"Imports are over-priced," said Shim, the former senior adviser to finance minister Rha Woong-bae, who was replaced in August in a partial cabinet reshuffle.
